Gene Description

Cullin-3 is the central scaffold of CRL3 ubiquitin ligase complexes. Its N-terminal region recruits BTB/POZ-containing substrate adaptors, while its C-terminal region engages RBX1 and the ubiquitin-transfer machinery. These assemblies control protein abundance through ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal turnover and also generate non-degradative ubiquitin signals that regulate mitosis, membrane trafficking and other substrate-specific processes. CUL3 acts in nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments, with regulated Golgi, membrane and mitotic pools. Adaptor choice couples the same scaffold to targets involved in oxidative-stress responses, cell-cycle control, receptor and metabolic signaling, and transcriptional regulation. The displayed 768-residue product and two shorter splice products differ in the N-terminal adaptor-binding region: the 744-residue product lacks residues 1–24 and the 702-residue product lacks residues 23–88 of the displayed sequence.

Core Functions

Assemble CRL3 ubiquitin ligases by binding BTB/POZ substrate adaptors through the CUL3 N terminus and RBX1 through its C-terminal region. This scaffold contributes to substrate ubiquitination, including proteasomal targeting in degradative assemblies and non-degradative regulation in other adaptor contexts. It does not independently catalyze ubiquitin transfer, neddylation or proteolysis. BTB/POZ-domain binding is the substrate-adaptor recruitment component of this coordinated assembly function.

Molecular Function:
ubiquitin ligase complex scaffold activity
Directly Involved In:
protein ubiquitination proteasome-mediated ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolic process
Cellular Locations:
cytosol nucleus
In Complex:
Cul3-RING ubiquitin ligase complex

Suggested Questions for Experts

Q: Which CUL3 splice products assemble functional CRL3 complexes in specific tissues, and how do the N-terminal deletions alter adaptor affinity or substrate selection? Historical exon-deletion baits and disease-associated internal deletions are not equivalent to all three official products.

Q: Under which endogenous-protein, epitope-tag, antibody and nutrient-medium conditions does KLHL22 promote DEPDC5 turnover? The original report, later challenge and reply leave the substrate-specific mechanism unresolved.

Suggested Experiments

Experiment: Compare purified full-length Q13618-1, Q13618-2 and Q13618-3 at matched protein concentrations for binding to selected BTB adaptors, RBX1 assembly and substrate-directed ubiquitination. Include the historical bait boundaries separately rather than treating them as full splice products.

Experiment: Test endogenous DEPDC5 turnover and mTORC1 outputs across matched DMEM and RPMI starvation/refeeding protocols, using validated antibodies, untagged controls and independent KLHL22 perturbations. Quantify any cleaved or selectively regulated DEPDC5 pool.

Concise GO annotation research report: Human CUL3 (Cullin-3; UniProt Q13618) — GO-relevant evidence only

Scope and annotation philosophy

This report summarizes evidence supporting core Gene Ontology (GO) annotations for human CUL3 as a cullin–RING E3 ubiquitin ligase scaffold (CRL3). Emphasis is on direct molecular function (MF), complex assembly/cellular component (CC), and proximal biological processes (BP) (ubiquitination and ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis), while downstream phenotypes/pathway roles (oxidative stress response, blood pressure, neurodevelopment, cancer, viral infection) are treated as non-core unless the evidence directly establishes CUL3’s mechanistic role.

1) Key concepts and definitions (current understanding)

CUL3 as a cullin–RING E3 ligase scaffold (GO: MF/CC core)

CUL3 is the central scaffold of CRL3 ubiquitin ligases, bridging (i) a RING protein (RBX1) that recruits E2~ubiquitin and (ii) BTB-domain substrate adaptor/receptor proteins that recruit specific substrates. This architecture is described in recent mechanistic reviews and supported by primary structural work, including explicit CUL3–RBX1 and adaptor-bound complexes (jeong2023targetinge3ubiquitin pages 2-3, sharma2023insightsintothe pages 1-3, hu2024dynamicmoleculararchitecture pages 1-21).

Direct structural/biochemical evidence includes:
- Cryo-EM showing CRL3 assemblies containing CUL3 + RBX1 + BTB adaptor (e.g., KLHL22-based CRL3) and supporting the concept that dimerization of BTB adaptors yields a 2:2 stoichiometry (BTB dimer recruiting two CUL3–RBX1 arms) that supports ligase activity (wang2024aconservednterminal pages 1-2, wang2024aconservednterminal pages 7-8).
- KEAP1–CUL3 crystal structure evidence of a heterotetrameric 2:2 complex (KEAP1:CUL3) with quantitative binding (KD ~0.2 μM), reinforcing the scaffold/adaptor binding model (preprint) (adamson2023structuralandbiochemical pages 1-7).

GO MF term guidance: evidence best supports a CUL3 annotation consistent with “ubiquitin ligase complex scaffold activity” / E3 ligase scaffold rather than “ubiquitin-protein transferase activity” (which is catalytic and typically attributed to the E2/E3 catalytic machinery rather than the scaffold) (jeong2023targetinge3ubiquitin pages 2-3, wang2024aconservednterminal pages 1-2).

Assembly of CRL3 complexes with RBX1 and BTB adaptors (GO: CC and complex assembly)

Recent structural work shows that CRL3s are multi-subunit complexes with physically resolved interfaces that underlie assembly.
- A May 2024 cryo-EM/biochemistry study on CRL3^KLHL22 identifies a conserved N-terminal motif in CUL3 that contributes to dimeric CRL3 assembly and E3 activity; deletion reduces adaptor binding and changes complex stoichiometry (wang2024aconservednterminal pages 7-8, wang2024aconservednterminal pages 1-2).
- Feb 2024 cryo-EM structural states of CRL3^KBTBD2 include substrate-engaged forms and regulatory complexes with the COP9 signalosome and CAND1, supporting CUL3’s role as a structural platform that coordinates catalytic and regulatory modules (hu2024dynamicmoleculararchitecture pages 1-21).

2) Recent developments and latest research (prioritize 2023–2024)

2024 cryo-EM reveals CRL3 architecture, substrate recruitment, and regulation

A 2024 Nature Structural & Molecular Biology study provides multiple cryo-EM reconstructions of CRL3^KBTBD2 including:
- A neddylated CRL3 form (CUL3~NEDD8),
- complexes with the COP9 signalosome (CSN) (including mutant CSN states), and
- a CUL3–RBX1–CAND1 complex.
These structures directly support GO-relevant assertions that CRL3 activity is coupled to neddylation/deneddylation and regulated by exchange factors such as CAND1 (hu2024dynamicmoleculararchitecture pages 1-21).

2023–2024 tools to measure activated (neddylated) CRLs in cells

A 2023 Nature Chemical Biology study developed a conformation-specific probe recognizing NEDD8-linked active cullins and profiled activated CRL networks including CUL3-containing complexes (henneberg2023activitybasedprofilingof pages 1-2). The work includes experimental perturbations with MLN4924 (NAE inhibitor; blocks neddylation) and CSN5i-3 (blocks deneddylation), and explicitly detects NEDD8–CUL3 species by IP–MS (henneberg2023activitybasedprofilingof pages 6-6). This supports GO-relevant statements that (i) neddylation activates CRLs and (ii) active-state abundance is dynamically regulated.

2024 synthesis of structural knowledge on neddylation regulators (CSN, CAND1)

A 2024 review in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy compiles recent structures that include CUL3–KLHL22–RBX1, CAND1–CUL3–RBX1, and KBTBD2–NEDD8–CUL3–RBX1–CSN assemblies (listed PDBs/EM structures), and emphasizes that CSN removes NEDD8 whereas CAND1 preferentially binds unneddylated cullins as a negative regulator/exchange factor (zhang2024proteinneddylationand pages 8-10). (Review-level evidence; use primarily to support general regulatory concepts rather than highly specific GO regulator terms.)

3) Current applications and real-world implementations (GO-relevant)

While not GO terms per se, applications inform which mechanistic aspects are robustly established.

  • Pharmacologic modulation of CRL3 activity via neddylation: MLN4924 is widely used to inhibit NEDD8-activating enzyme (NAE), thereby inhibiting CRL activity; CUL3-linked CRL activity is described as requiring neddylation in multiple contexts (henneberg2023activitybasedprofilingof pages 6-6, gu2024cullin3ring pages 1-2).
  • Targeted protein degradation and E3 ligase engagement: CRL3 adaptors such as KEAP1 appear in degrader/TPD discussions as E3 components that can be recruited in chemical biology approaches; this supports the practical importance of accurate annotation of CRL3 scaffold/adaptor assembly, though it does not add new GO terms (jeong2023targetinge3ubiquitin pages 2-3).

4) Expert opinions and analysis: GO annotation recommendations and caveats

Core GO: Molecular function

Strongly supported (core):
- Ubiquitin ligase complex scaffold activity / E3 ubiquitin ligase scaffold — CUL3 is repeatedly defined and structurally demonstrated as a CRL scaffold bridging RBX1 and BTB adaptors, including detailed stoichiometry and interface determinants (wang2024aconservednterminal pages 1-2, adamson2023structuralandbiochemical pages 1-7, hu2024dynamicmoleculararchitecture pages 1-21).

Caution:
- Avoid annotating CUL3 with generic “protein binding” or “ubiquitin protein ligase binding” unless the evidence is specifically required for MF, because these terms are often low-information and may reflect experimental detection rather than biological specificity.

Core GO: Biological process

Strongly supported (core/proximal):
- Protein ubiquitination / protein polyubiquitination: Multiple CRL3 systems demonstrate ubiquitination output; for example, CRL3^KLHL22 assays support ubiquitination activity dependence on CUL3 structural motifs (wang2024aconservednterminal pages 1-2), and CRL3^KCTD7 demonstrates CUL3-dependent ubiquitination of calpains (sengupta2023theubiquitinlikeproteins pages 4-5).

Proteasome-mediated ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolic process (supported, but adaptor/substrate-dependent):
- Proteasomal targeting is a canonical outcome for many CRLs, and reviews explicitly describe substrate ubiquitination “for proteasomal degradation” as a CRL3 output (sharma2023insightsintothe pages 1-3). However, not all CUL3-dependent ubiquitination is degradative (see KCTD7/calpain below), so proteasome-related BP annotations should be supported by substrate degradation evidence rather than ubiquitination alone.

Critical caveat (avoid over-annotation):
- Non-degradative ubiquitination: the KCTD7–CUL3–RBX1 complex ubiquitinates calpains with atypical chain linkages (K6/K27/K29/K63) and regulates activity rather than proteasomal turnover; this supports “protein ubiquitination” but argues against automatically applying proteasome-mediated catabolism for all CUL3-dependent ubiquitination (sengupta2023theubiquitinlikeproteins pages 4-5).
- Pathway membership / phenotype-only evidence: oxidative stress response, blood pressure/electrolyte phenotypes, neurodevelopmental phenotypes, or cancer-associated phenotypes can be downstream of CUL3-dependent substrate regulation. These should not be treated as core CUL3 BP terms without direct mechanistic evidence that CUL3’s scaffold activity is required in the specific pathway node being annotated.

Core GO: Cellular component

Supported (core):
- Cul3-RING ubiquitin ligase complex / cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase complex: direct structural evidence places CUL3 in CRL3 assemblies containing RBX1 and BTB adaptors (hu2024dynamicmoleculararchitecture pages 1-21, wang2024aconservednterminal pages 1-2).

Cytosol/cytoplasm and nucleus (plausible but evidence here is limited):
- A 2024 preprint reports differential tumor-context localization of CUL3 (cytoplasmic in one subtype; nuclear/perinuclear in another) and suggests nuclear engagement via interactions with RNA polymerase complexes in DNA damage contexts (pantazi2024ubiquitylationmediatedrnapiigenomic pages 100-104). Because this is preprint-level and partially inference-based, it supports a cautious note that CUL3 can be found in cytoplasmic and nuclear contexts but may not be sufficient alone for strong CC annotations.

Membrane/centrosome/cytoskeleton claims require caution:
- A 2024 structure paper on CRL3^KCTD5 describes compatibility with membrane-bound Gβγ in the reaction complex; this is substrate-contextual and does not justify annotating CUL3 broadly as a membrane component (jeong2023targetinge3ubiquitin pages 2-3).
- No strong direct evidence in the retrieved set supports centrosome or cytoskeleton localization as a general CC term for CUL3; references to kinetochores/mitosis are often substrate-contextual and may reflect downstream phenotype or adaptor targeting rather than stable CUL3 localization.

5) Relevant statistics and data (recent studies)

  • Stoichiometry data: structural/biochemical studies support 2:2 assemblies (BTB dimer with two CUL3 arms) in CRL3 complexes and provide measurable changes in complex stoichiometry when CUL3 motifs are deleted (wang2024aconservednterminal pages 1-2, wang2024aconservednterminal pages 7-8). KEAP1–CUL3 binding is reported with KD ~0.2 μM and a 2:2 heterotetramer in structural/biochemical assays (preprint) (adamson2023structuralandbiochemical pages 1-7).
  • Network scale estimate: a 2023 review states mammals may form up to 188 distinct CUL3–BTB E3 complexes, underscoring annotation relevance for “CUL3-RING ubiquitin ligase complex” rather than overly specific pathway terms (jeong2023targetinge3ubiquitin pages 2-3).
  • Quantitative profiling of NEDD8–CUL3: IP–MS profiling explicitly detects “NEDD8–CUL3” and uses inhibitors (MLN4924; CSN5i-3) to modulate neddylation/deneddylation states, providing empirical support that CUL3 participates in dynamic neddylation-regulated CRL activation (henneberg2023activitybasedprofilingof pages 6-6).

GO-relevant adaptor/substrate examples (evidence-weighted)

The table below summarizes adaptor modules and indicates which are core vs cautionary for CUL3 GO inference.

Table: This table summarizes direct GO-relevant evidence for human CUL3 across key CRL3 adaptor systems, highlighting what supports core scaffold and ubiquitination annotations versus what should be treated cautiously as adaptor-specific, non-degradative, or phenotype-driven.

Summary: Recommended core GO assertions for CUL3 (evidence-backed)

  1. MF: ubiquitin ligase complex scaffold activity (CRL3 scaffold) supported by multiple 2023–2024 structural/biochemical studies (wang2024aconservednterminal pages 1-2, hu2024dynamicmoleculararchitecture pages 1-21, adamson2023structuralandbiochemical pages 1-7).
  2. CC: member of Cul3-RING ubiquitin ligase complex / CRL3 complexes with RBX1 and BTB adaptors (hu2024dynamicmoleculararchitecture pages 1-21, wang2024aconservednterminal pages 1-2).
  3. BP: protein ubiquitination and, in contexts with demonstrated degradative ubiquitination, protein polyubiquitination and proteasome-mediated ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolic process—while explicitly recognizing that some CRL3 outputs are non-degradative (wang2024aconservednterminal pages 1-2, sengupta2023theubiquitinlikeproteins pages 4-5, sharma2023insightsintothe pages 1-3).
  4. Regulation of activity: reversible neddylation activates CRLs; deneddylation (CSN) and exchange regulation via CAND1 are structurally supported for CUL3 complexes and experimentally manipulable in cells (hu2024dynamicmoleculararchitecture pages 1-21, henneberg2023activitybasedprofilingof pages 6-6, sharma2023insightsintothe pages 1-3, zhang2024proteinneddylationand pages 8-10).

📚 Additional Documentation

Notes

(CUL3-notes.md)

CUL3 notes

Initial Falcon pass, 2026-05-12. CUL3 started as a fully pending review with
228 annotations. I kept this pass centered on the conserved CRL3 scaffold
function and left most generic protein-binding and substrate-specific rows for
later source-level review.

Core molecular function: CUL3 is the scaffold of cullin-RING E3 ligase
complexes. Falcon states that CUL3 bridges RBX1/E2 ubiquitin-conjugating
machinery with BTB-domain substrate adaptors
[file:human/CUL3/CUL3-deep-research-falcon.md "CUL3 is the central
scaffold of CRL3 ubiquitin ligases, bridging (i) a RING protein (RBX1)
that recruits E2~ubiquitin and (ii) BTB-domain substrate adaptor/receptor
proteins that recruit specific substrates."]. I accepted ubiquitin ligase
complex scaffold activity and Cul3-RING ubiquitin ligase complex rows as the
core axis.

Core process: protein ubiquitination, polyubiquitination, and
proteasome-mediated ubiquitin-dependent catabolism are proximal outputs of many
CRL3 complexes [file:human/CUL3/CUL3-deep-research-falcon.md "Proteasomal
targeting is a canonical outcome for many CRLs, and reviews explicitly describe
substrate ubiquitination “for proteasomal degradation” as a CRL3 output"]. I
accepted well-supported ubiquitination and catabolic-process rows, but kept the
caveat that not every CUL3 ubiquitination event is degradative.

Molecular-function specificity: Falcon cautions that CUL3 is best represented
as the scaffold rather than the catalytic ubiquitin transferase
[file:human/CUL3/CUL3-deep-research-falcon.md "evidence best supports a CUL3
annotation consistent with “ubiquitin ligase complex scaffold activity” /
E3 ligase scaffold rather than “ubiquitin-protein transferase activity”
(which is catalytic and typically attributed to the E2/E3 catalytic machinery
rather than the scaffold)"]. I therefore modified ubiquitin-protein transferase
and ubiquitin protein ligase activity rows to the scaffold term.

Non-core contexts: many CUL3 annotations reflect the substrate/adaptor being
studied: KEAP1/NRF2 oxidative stress, KLHL3/WNK ion transport, KLHL12/COPII,
KBTBD/KCTD complexes, mitotic substrates, neuronal phenotypes, viral processes,
and disease models. Falcon warns that broad phenotypes should not be promoted
to core CUL3 functions without direct mechanistic evidence
[file:human/CUL3/CUL3-deep-research-falcon.md "oxidative stress response,
blood pressure/electrolyte phenotypes, neurodevelopmental phenotypes, or
cancer-associated phenotypes can be downstream of CUL3-dependent substrate
regulation. These should not be treated as core CUL3 BP terms without direct
mechanistic evidence that CUL3’s scaffold activity is required in the specific
pathway node being annotated."].

Localization: CUL3 complex membership is core. I accepted a few broad
cytoplasm/cytosol/nuclear rows, but Falcon notes that specific membrane,
centrosome, cytoskeleton, and other locations require caution
[file:human/CUL3/CUL3-deep-research-falcon.md "Membrane/centrosome/cytoskeleton
claims require caution:"]. Most highly specific or repetitive localization
rows remain pending unless a direct source was already strong enough for a
non-core decision.

Left for later: generic protein-binding rows should be triaged by partner
(BTB/POZ adaptor, RBX1, substrate, CSN/CAND1 regulator, or nonspecific
interaction). Substrate-specific phenotype rows should be reviewed one adaptor
module at a time rather than treated as core CUL3 biology.

Source-based augmentation, October 2026

The earlier Falcon-centered pass above is preserved as history. Its blanket catalytic refinements are superseded here: the source annotations explicitly qualified contributes_to are valid contributions to assembled ubiquitin transfer. CUL3 itself performs scaffold activity, linking BTB adaptors to RBX1/E2 machinery. The genuine Falcon report remains unchanged and was assessed as secondary background, not treated as an experimental source. PMID:14528312 and the actual PMID:20389280 reconstitution support this distinction. The compact core records one scaffold unit, its complex contribution, CRL3 membership, protein ubiquitination and proteasomal catabolism; it does not duplicate the nested polyubiquitination process or imply that all ubiquitination is degradative.

All 228 historical source objects are retained exactly, including qualifiers, absent defaults and tested-product fields. The preserved GOA has 383 raw rows; the genuine fresh seed has 375 rows, with different multiplicity, and the independent current QuickGO capture has 400. Those observations are not combined into a fabricated GOA. All three official products reconstruct exactly (768, 744 and 702 residues). The latter products delete residues 1–24 and 23–88, respectively. Historical 17–768 yeast bait and exon-deletion bait, artificial 34–74 deletion and the disease-associated 403–459 deletion remain separate construct contexts; equal function of all products is not established.

Actual PTHR11932 topology includes the exact CUL3 sequence and all six source IBDs on its ancestral path, with no target-path loss. Three historical/current donor sets differ, which is recorded without rewriting the historical source. Donor count and target self-evidence are not reasons to reject a PAINT inference. Complete donor pagination, literal source/term joins and all current ARBA branches were reconstructed. The adult mouse kidney-deletion source PMID:25250572 establishes injury and homeostasis, not embryonic kidney development; the COPII source PMID:22358839 establishes performed export regulation, without proving every downstream integrin, division or cleavage process.

The 57 interaction assertions were assessed against 1,466 IntAct and 91 MINT records, 262 used records and 524 exact sequence ROGIDs. This identity reconstruction does not prove every interaction is direct or physiological. Supported generic binding is retained as non-core under the standing ClinGen instruction; a measured partner/domain permits a more precise binding term. Source-specific interactions without an adjudicated target assay remain undecided. COPS5 enzyme binding, HSP90AB1 binding, ACOT7 thioesterase binding and experimentally mapped BTB contacts are refinements, not transfers of those partners' catalytic functions to CUL3.

Several original distinctions matter. PMID:25619834 supports RBX1/KLHL20 binding but reports failure of wild-type IVNS1ABP/KLHL39 to bind CUL3, with engineered substitutions restoring binding. Its original source tuple is preserved and the different partner arm is explained. PMID:38225382 measures positive KCTD7 BRET yet rejects the predicted interface for validation; it does not establish an isolated BTB interface. PMID:23455478 concerns KLHL22/PLK1 localization control, whereas PMID:22358839 concerns KLHL12/SEC31/collagen export. PMID:27561354 concerns KLHL15/CtIP, not KBTBD7. The positive nuclear CtIP turnover result does not establish misfolded-protein quality control, and the free-cyclin-E pathway of PMID:10500095 is not APC/C-dependent.

The original PMID:29769719 KLHL22–DEPDC5 mechanism is disputed by PMID:39780017 and defended in PMID:39780003. The challenge maintained cells in DMEM but used RPMI for its 50-minute starvation and 10-minute refeeding protocol. The reply invokes antibody, cleavage, tagging and medium differences and a regulated DEPDC5 subset. The challenge does not rule out ubiquitin regulation generally. The evidence does not settle the specific nutrient-response/TORC1 assertions; these remain undecided. Independently established CRL3 scaffold and proteasomal roles are retained without treating the disputed DEPDC5 route as a settled example. The paper is not labeled retracted or invalid.

Positive mitotic, centrosomal, Golgi and partner-recruited membrane pools are retained at their actual source scope. Human CUL3 knockdown, reconstitution and localization in the Aurora/PLK1/KLHL42 studies support contextual participation, not intrinsic kinase or microtubule catalytic activity. Non-degradative SEC31, Aurora and TCOF1/NOLC1 modifications remain distinct from proteasomal targeting. The urinary-exosome database supporting PMID:19056867 contains a single-peptide CUL3/NP_003581 identification at zero-based HTML row 325, reference 2; it establishes detection, not secretion or extracellular function. The unresolved YTS membrane screen is not rescued merely by independent plasma-membrane recruitment in another experiment.

All 15 target GO-CAM activities place CUL3 in the scaffold role with separate neighboring adaptor/catalytic roles. A bounded current Reactome reconstruction authenticated 521 objects, 700 edges and 42 Q13618 target paths; 31 nested IDs remain unresolved after genuine access failures and a fixed retry budget. The compact evidence index distinguishes those incomplete paths from reached target paths. Cached event context and independent localization can support the existing broad compartment assertions, but missing objects are not negative evidence and neighboring deneddylase, NEDD8-transferase, proteasome or adaptor functions are not transferred to CUL3.

ROOT independently read the two-source catalytic-contribution slice, five ARMC5 sources and the KLHL22 dispute; their complete reports and exact source bindings were read and reproduced by the owner. Other personally read primary windows are recorded in the owner source ledger, with explicit limits for abstracts, selected full-text paragraphs, author reprints and inaccessible supplementary assays. The 19782033 erratum contents remain unavailable. References 29249570, 31898230 and 37628845 are reviews, not new primary assays. An available cache or an exact interaction ID does not imply that every target table or figure was read.

The current review replaces the former 318 provider-centered/repeated support items with source-specific support and a small set of literal primary anchors. This is not a claim that all quote leaves are unchanged: the original review and this notes prefix retain their historical wording. Newly authored primary quotations are checked against unchanged caches and limited to 25 words per source across their occurrences; this appendix adds no primary quotation. No NEW annotation is proposed.

Whole-review precision corrections

The independent whole review identified one source-specific action correction. Row 207 is now UNDECIDED: the complete PMID:18826954 abstract and current interaction exports do not resolve its CUL3–DCUN1D1 assay. The paper-specific reference assessment is UNVERIFIED, while the genuine positive association established by separate DCNL–CUL3 studies remains acknowledged. This is an access and evidence limit, not a claim of nonbinding. The final actions are 112 ACCEPT, 73 KEEP_AS_NON_CORE, 21 MODIFY, 13 UNDECIDED and 9 MARK_AS_OVER_ANNOTATED.

Three prose corrections identify GO_REF:0000002 as InterPro-to-GO, place the DCDC2C emphasis in the PMID:28395323 abstract, and distinguish the PMID:18397884 abstract's CUL3-dependent TIP60 result from an unrecovered literal interaction record. Row 176 remains supported through the same-paper functional evidence and curated IPI, without claiming a recovered target pair. All 228 historical source objects, 132 reference identifiers/titles, three product objects and the core model remain unchanged.

The preceding support-consolidation statement describes the first whole draft. The final review restores the exact inherited PMID:24145166 Golgi-localization excerpt once on row 86. Its old duplicate on row 11 and the redundant RhoBTB3–cyclin-E sentence remain omitted; the two old PMID:14528312 excerpts do not resolve the distinct autoubiquitination assay and remain omitted. The 312 former Falcon support items are replaced by source-specific assessment, while the genuine Falcon document stays protected. The restored Golgi excerpt is inherited repository text, separately tracked from the ten newly selected primary anchors; no new quotation is added by this appendix.

CUL3 finite external-review follow-up

The published source objects, all annotation actions, three products, existing support excerpts and one integrated core are retained. Extracellular-exosome row 171 remains KEEP_AS_NON_CORE because the original urinary-exosome table reports the exact CUL3 target; the one-peptide identification is limited evidence for a preparation-specific compartment, not evidence of a secretion mechanism or extracellular enzymatic role. Neither of the latter is required by the cellular-component term. PMID:19056867 is now MEDIUM relevance, while unrecovered CUL3-specific screen records in PMID:19946888 and PMID:40205054 are LOW relevance and remain UNVERIFIED.

The core explicitly incorporates BTB/POZ adaptor engagement within the scaffold assembly activity. GO:0160072 already describes bringing together an ubiquitin ligase and its substrate adaptor. The accepted POZ-domain binding refinements are preserved and supported in that same functional unit; no second copy of this assembly step is added solely because the same binding term occurs in multiple source rows.

The new CUL3-primary-source-notes.md gives DOI, printed-page and section locators for the adult renal study and both KLHL22 letters, with short exact anchors from the original PDFs. It corrects the previous row 65 statement: nephron qPCR maps Klhl3/Cul3 expression, whereas the adult-deletion work mainly measures protein abundance, phosphorylation and renal physiology. This does not establish CUL3 performing gene expression, so the source-specific over-annotation remains; no contrary experiment is invented. The independent stem-cell and cleavage source is PMID:22358839. Original publication caches and previous notes are unchanged.

GO_REF assessments now describe their particular mapping or inference methods. The screen-table access task formerly posed as the third expert question belongs here: unresolved interactions, homomeric binding and autoubiquitination require the original target assays before their uncertainty can be closed. Existing biological isoform and KLHL22 questions remain. Authored index spacing is corrected without changing literal source identifiers. The historical notes prefix and history records remain intact; prior text is superseded only where this appendix explicitly corrects it.

Primary Source Notes

(CUL3-primary-source-notes.md)

CUL3 primary-source assay notes

These notes make three source-specific judgments locally checkable without replacing the publication caches. The original PDF text and the identified figure captions were inspected. Figure pixels and separate supplements were not newly inspected for this follow-up. The two 2025 letters appeared together in the retrieved PDF; they are opposing interpretations, not independent confirmations.

PMID:25250572 — adult renal deletion and expression measurements

Original JCI article, J Clin Invest. 2014;124:4723–4736; original PDF; PMC4347254.

  • Design: printed p. 4724, final Introduction paragraph; p. 4728, the Results paragraph introducing kidney-specific deletion; pp. 4734–4735, Animals and dietary Methods. The experiment deletes Cul3 along the nephron after normal development using doxycycline-controlled Pax8/TRE-LC1 recombination. The stated restriction is “only in adult mice”. The short-term dietary experiment uses mice aged 2–3 months. It tests adult maintenance and physiology, rather than embryonic kidney morphogenesis.
  • Inflammation: printed p. 4730, Results describing chronic kidney damage; p. 4734, Figure 8 caption. Histology identifies tubulointerstitial inflammation, fibrosis, neutrophils and white-cell casts following deletion. This establishes an injury-associated inflammatory outcome; it does not isolate a step of inflammatory response performed by CUL3.
  • Expression: printed pp. 4727–4728, Figure 4 caption and Results on nephron expression; p. 4735, nephron-segment PCR Methods. The authors quantify Klhl3 and Cul3 transcripts across isolated nephron segments, describing Cul3 as showing “modest and relatively uniform expression”. This is expression of the measured genes. The deletion Results use Western blotting/immunofluorescence to assess WNK kinases, transporters and phosphorylation, alongside electrolyte and physiological endpoints. The previous row 65 wording about altered renal transcript levels after deletion was too specific and is superseded. These measurements do not identify CUL3 itself as executing transcription, RNA processing or translation.

The kidney-development, inflammatory-response and gene-expression transfers remain source-specific over-annotations. This is not a general rejection of other CUL3 developmental or transcription-related biology. The stem-cell-division and embryonic-cleavage judgments cite a different paper, PMID:22358839, and must not be attributed to this renal experiment.

PMID:39780017 — challenge to KLHL22–DEPDC5 turnover

Original challenge, Nature 2025;637:E11–E14; PDF.

Printed p. E11 describes antibody validation using DEPDC5-knockout and endogenous 3×Flag-tagged HEK293T cells. The authors report that validated endogenous DEPDC5 signals do not change as proposed under amino-acid, proteasome-inhibition or KLHL22-loss conditions. Printed p. E12, Figure 1 caption and ensuing text, identifies the measured immunoblot and signaling endpoints. These are the challenge's reported findings, not a new analysis of its image pixels.

Printed p. E13, Cell lines and tissue culture plus Transfection and cell lysis Methods, distinguishes routine culture in DMEM from the starvation/refeeding protocol: “amino-acid-free RPMI for 50 min”, followed by amino-acid addition for 10 minutes. Printed p. E11, final main paragraph, expressly leaves broader ubiquitin regulation of mTORC1 possible while challenging the proposed acute DEPDC5-degradation mechanism. Its result should not be paraphrased as disproving every ubiquitin-dependent effect.

PMID:39780003 — reply and remaining uncertainty

Original reply, Nature 2025;637:E15–E17; PDF.

Printed p. E15 discusses antibody/cleavage interpretation and potential effects of endogenous epitope tagging. Printed pp. E15–E16, the nutrient-treatment paragraph and Figure 1i caption, contrast the reply's use of DMEM for culture and amino-acid treatments with the challenge's switch to RPMI. Printed p. E16, Figure 1j–l caption, describes the proposed ubiquitination/degradation evidence and model; printed p. E17, concluding paragraph, restricts that model to “a subset of DEPDC5”. These proposed reagent, tagging and condition explanations do not establish that either report is universally applicable.

Accordingly, PMID:29769719 remains DISPUTED, with both challenge and reply named. The specific amino-acid-response and TORC1-regulation assertions remain UNDECIDED. Broad CUL3 scaffold and proteasomal-turnover functions retain their independent experimental support; the contested DEPDC5 route is not used as their sole justification. No retraction or universal nonbinding/degradation conclusion is asserted.

references:
- id: GO_REF:0000002
  title: Gene Ontology annotation through association of InterPro records with GO terms
  findings: []
  reference_review:
    relevance: HIGH
    correctness: VERIFIED
    review_notes: InterPro-to-GO mapping is the source of these electronic assertions. The literal InterPro
      identifiers and the claimed catabolic or ligase-binding scope were assessed; this mapping is not
      a PAINT result or a primary assay.
- id: GO_REF:0000024
  title: Manual transfer of experimentally-verified manual GO annotation data to orthologs by curator
    judgment of sequence similarity
  findings: []
  reference_review:
    relevance: HIGH
    correctness: VERIFIED
    review_notes: Manual curator transfer by orthology supplies the three ISS process assertions. The
      literal donor and its experimental process evidence were assessed separately; collagen-export or
      integrin phenotypes do not automatically establish every transferred division/signaling role.
- id: GO_REF:0000033
  title: Annotation inferences using phylogenetic trees
  findings: []
  reference_review:
    relevance: HIGH
    correctness: VERIFIED
    review_notes: PAINT inheritance was reconstructed from the actual PTHR11932 tree, target alignment,
      on-path IBD nodes and literal descendant evidence. This is phylogenetic inference, including legitimate
      target self-evidence, rather than an independent human experiment.
- id: GO_REF:0000044
  title: Gene Ontology annotation based on UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot Subcellular Location vocabulary mapping,
    accompanied by conservative changes to GO terms applied by UniProt
  findings: []
  reference_review:
    relevance: HIGH
    correctness: VERIFIED
    review_notes: These electronic cellular-component assertions derive from UniProt subcellular-location
      vocabulary mapping. The literal location source and target-specific localization evidence were assessed,
      rather than treating the method reference as a primary imaging paper.
- id: GO_REF:0000052
  title: Gene Ontology annotation based on curation of immunofluorescence data
  findings: []
  reference_review:
    relevance: HIGH
    correctness: VERIFIED
    review_notes: These IDA location assertions arise from curated immunofluorescence data. The saved
      Human Protein Atlas CUL3 localization record was examined for nucleoplasm and microtubule-cytoskeleton
      context; neither PAINT nor ARBA is the source of this method.
- id: GO_REF:0000107
  title: Automatic transfer of experimentally verified manual GO annotation data to orthologs using Ensembl
    Compara
  findings: []
  reference_review:
    relevance: HIGH
    correctness: VERIFIED
    review_notes: Ensembl Compara automatic ortholog transfer supplies these electronic assertions. Complete
      literal donor-term joins were reconstructed and the linked experimental publications assessed for
      the exact target claim. Adult renal physiology and collagen-export phenotypes are kept distinct
      from inferred development or division.
- id: GO_REF:0000108
  title: Automatic assignment of GO terms using logical inference, based on on inter-ontology links
  findings: []
  reference_review:
    relevance: HIGH
    correctness: VERIFIED
    review_notes: The postsynapse annotation is an inter-ontology logical inference from a GO relationship,
      not an additional localization assay. Its general postsynaptic placement is assessed with the independently
      supported neuronal CUL3 context.
- id: GO_REF:0000117
  title: Electronic Gene Ontology annotations created by ARBA machine learning models
  findings: []
  reference_review:
    relevance: HIGH
    correctness: VERIFIED
    review_notes: ARBA machine-learning rules supply these electronic annotations. Actual rule predicates,
      taxon/domain conditions and matched branches were reconstructed; a matching rule is distinguished
      from experimental evidence for the named process.
- id: GO_REF:0000120
  title: Combined Automated Annotation using Multiple IEA Methods
  findings: []
  reference_review:
    relevance: HIGH
    correctness: VERIFIED
    review_notes: This reference denotes combined electronic annotation methods. The literal WITH/FROM
      mappings were retained and the applicable UniProt, InterPro and rule sources checked for each assertion;
      the combined label is not one uniform primary experiment.

- id: file:human/CUL3/CUL3-primary-source-notes.md
  title: CUL3 primary-source assay notes
  findings: []
  reference_review:
    relevance: HIGH
    correctness: VERIFIED
    review_notes: Authored analysis of three separately accessed original papers, with public DOI/PDF
      locators, exact printed-page/section references and bounded verbatim anchors. This is a source guide,
      not a replacement publication cache or a claim to have reviewed every figure or supplement.
core_functions:
- description: Assemble CRL3 ubiquitin ligases by binding BTB/POZ substrate adaptors through the CUL3
    N terminus and RBX1 through its C-terminal region. This scaffold contributes to substrate ubiquitination,
    including proteasomal targeting in degradative assemblies and non-degradative regulation in other
    adaptor contexts. It does not independently catalyze ubiquitin transfer, neddylation or proteolysis.
    BTB/POZ-domain binding is the substrate-adaptor recruitment component of this coordinated assembly
    function.
  molecular_function:
    id: GO:0160072
    label: ubiquitin ligase complex scaffold activity
  contributes_to_molecular_function:
    id: GO:0004842
    label: ubiquitin-protein transferase activity
  in_complex:
    id: GO:0031463
    label: Cul3-RING ubiquitin ligase complex
  directly_involved_in:
  - id: GO:0016567
    label: protein ubiquitination
  - id: GO:0043161
    label: proteasome-mediated ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolic process
  locations:
  - id: GO:0005829
    label: cytosol
  - id: GO:0005634
    label: nucleus
  supported_by:
  - reference_id: PMID:14528312
  - reference_id: PMID:20389280
  - reference_id: PMID:19995937
  - reference_id: PMID:22358839
  - reference_id: PMID:35687106
  - reference_id: PMID:15107402
  - reference_id: PMID:18573101
  - reference_id: PMID:26334369
proposed_new_terms: []
suggested_questions:
- question: Which CUL3 splice products assemble functional CRL3 complexes in specific tissues, and how
    do the N-terminal deletions alter adaptor affinity or substrate selection? Historical exon-deletion
    baits and disease-associated internal deletions are not equivalent to all three official products.
- question: Under which endogenous-protein, epitope-tag, antibody and nutrient-medium conditions does
    KLHL22 promote DEPDC5 turnover? The original report, later challenge and reply leave the substrate-specific
    mechanism unresolved.
suggested_experiments:
- description: Compare purified full-length Q13618-1, Q13618-2 and Q13618-3 at matched protein concentrations
    for binding to selected BTB adaptors, RBX1 assembly and substrate-directed ubiquitination. Include
    the historical bait boundaries separately rather than treating them as full splice products.
- description: Test endogenous DEPDC5 turnover and mTORC1 outputs across matched DMEM and RPMI starvation/refeeding
    protocols, using validated antibodies, untagged controls and independent KLHL22 perturbations. Quantify
    any cleaved or selectively regulated DEPDC5 pool.
status: DRAFT
